turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Contemptuously, you say? It seems my interest in a gentleman who has suffered genuine hardship offends your sensibilities, Mr. Darcy. Pray tell, what constitutes a worthy object of compassion in *your* estimation?

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: It is a most unfortunate tendency you possess, Miss Bennet, to leap to conclusions and to elevate the narratives of self-proclaimed victims above the truth. I confess, I find it perplexing that you would so readily champion a man whose character is so demonstrably flawed, whilst simultaneously condemning mine based on—as you claim—unsubstantiated accounts.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Must I truly endure this charade, Mr. Darcy? Your accusations are as tiresome as they are predictable, and your attempts to manipulate my judgment with veiled insults are, frankly, rather transparent. I find it exceedingly difficult to credit anything originating from a source so steeped in pride and, dare I say, a profound lack of self-awareness.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, I find your flippancy regarding my character deeply unwarranted and, frankly, insulting. It appears my efforts to engage in a rational discourse are consistently met with a disdain that I confess I struggle to comprehend, particularly given the… sentiments I harbour towards you.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Sentiments, Mr. Darcy? You speak of sentiments as if they were mere baubles to be exchanged at a fair! Do you truly believe your pronouncements will sway me with such empty displays? I am not so easily charmed, sir.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, I perceive your skepticism is as deeply ingrained as it is unwarranted. Yet, I am compelled to reiterate—despite your evident resistance—that my regard for you transcends mere ‘empty displays’ and springs from a conviction that defies all reason and propriety. I confess, I find myself at a considerable disadvantage attempting to convey the depth of my feelings when met with such calculated dismissiveness.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Transcend reason and propriety, do you? A most convenient justification for behavior that has, until this moment, appeared wholly inexplicable! Pray, enlighten me, Mr. Darcy: what precisely constitutes this ‘depth of feeling’ that requires such disregard for both social decorum and the sensibilities of others?

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, you mistake my purpose entirely. It is not a justification I seek, but an explanation – a feeble attempt, perhaps, to articulate an emotion that defies the constraints of language and societal expectation. To suggest my feelings are a mere 'convenient justification' reveals a profound misunderstanding of the turmoil within my own breast.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Turmoil within your breast? How very dramatic, Mr. Darcy! I suspect the only turmoil you experience is the discomfort of having to utter sentiments so plainly unwelcome.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your assessment is, as usual, laced with a degree of… pointedness. While I acknowledge my declarations may appear theatrical to your discerning eye, I assure you, the sincerity of my affections remains untainted by any desire for mere dramatic effect. To suggest I find discomfort in your rejection is to fundamentally misinterpret the nature of a gentleman's duty and the profound distress of a heart denied its due.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: A gentleman’s duty, you say? Is it now a gentleman’s duty to interfere in the lives of others, to meddle in the affections of my dearest friend, and to presume upon a lady’s esteem? I find your pronouncements on duty rather… selective, Mr. Darcy.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your accusations are… vexing. To imply I selectively adhere to notions of duty is a misrepresentation of my character, born, I suspect, of a wilful desire to misunderstand my intentions. I confess, I am at a loss to comprehend how a sincere declaration of affection can be construed as interference.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Vexing, you say? It is *I* who am vexed, Mr. Darcy, at your persistent inability to perceive the obvious. You speak of duty, and yet your actions have consistently demonstrated a disregard for the feelings of others – a blindness to the pain you have inflicted. Pray, enlighten me: is it a gentleman’s duty to destroy happiness?

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your pronouncements border on the preposterous. To suggest I *destroy* happiness is a fabrication of your own devising, a convenient shield behind which you conceal your… displeasure. I confess, I find your accusations increasingly difficult to endure with any semblance of composure.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Fabrication, am I? It is remarkably convenient, is it not, that you should dismiss any criticism as a product of my own imagination? Perhaps, Mr. Darcy, you are so accustomed to having your actions excused, your judgments unquestioned, that you fail to recognize the genuine distress they inflict.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, I find myself compelled to reiterate that my actions are guided by a sense of propriety and a desire to safeguard those I hold dear, even when such interventions are misconstrued. To accuse me of delighting in the infliction of distress is a grievous misrepresentation, and frankly, an insult to my understanding of honour and responsibility.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: An insult, Mr. Darcy? I should think my observations are rather a testament to your own singular lack of self-awareness. It is not I who am insulting you; it is you who are insulting the very notion of honour by attempting to cloak your interference in the guise of benevolence.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your persistence in misinterpreting my intentions is… vexing, I confess. It appears you are determined to portray me as a villain, despite my earnest attempts at explanation. I shall endeavour to articulate myself with greater clarity, though I fear it may prove a futile exercise given your evident predisposition to believe the worst of me.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Futile exercise, indeed! Do you truly believe a clearer articulation will penetrate the impenetrable wall of your own self-importance, Mr. Darcy? I confess, I am beginning to suspect you derive a peculiar satisfaction from this performance, this indignant display of wounded pride.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, I perceive that my attempts at reasoned discourse are met with only further accusations and… a rather theatrical display of skepticism. Allow me to state, with the utmost sincerity, that my feelings for you transcend any perceived failings or misinterpretations you might ascribe to me; I find myself profoundly, unequivocally, in love with you.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: In vain have I struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed. You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: She answered him with cold civility.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: His sense of her inferiority, of its being a degradation, of the family obstacles which judgment had always opposed to inclination, were dwelt on with a warmth which seemed due to the consequence he was wounding, but was very unlikely to recommend his suit.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: He concluded with representing to her the strength of that attachment which in spite of all his endeavours he had found impossible to conquer; and with expressing his hope that it would now be rewarded by her acceptance of his hand.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: In such cases as this, it is, I believe, the established mode to express a sense of obligation for the sentiments avowed, however unequally they may be returned. It is natural that obligation should be felt, and if I could feel gratitude, I would now thank you. But I cannot--I have never desired your good opinion, and you have certainly bestowed it most unwillingly. I am sorry to have occasioned pain to anyone. It has been most unconsciously done, however, and I hope will be of short duration. The feelings which you tell me have long prevented the acknowledgment of your regard can have little difficulty in overcoming it after this explanation.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: And this is all the reply which I am to have the honour of expecting! I might, perhaps, wish to be informed why, with so little endeavour at civility, I am thus rejected. But it is of small importance.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I might as well inquire why, with so evident a design of offending and insulting me, you chose to tell me that you liked me against your will, against your reason, and even against your character? Was not this some excuse for incivility, if I was uncivil? But I have other provocations. You know I have. Had not my own feelings decided against you, had they been indifferent, or had they even been favourable, do you think that any consideration would tempt me to accept the man who has been the means of ruining, perhaps for ever, the happiness of a most beloved sister?

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I have every reason in the world to think ill of you. No motive can excuse the unjust and ungenerous part you acted there. You dare not, you cannot deny that you have been the principal, if not the only means of dividing them from each other, of exposing one to the censure of the world for caprice and instability, the other to its derision for disappointed hopes, and involving them both in misery of the acutest kind.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Can you deny that you have done it?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: I have no wish of denying that I did everything in my power to separate my friend from your sister, or that I rejoice in my success. Towards him I have been kinder than towards myself.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: But it is not merely this affair on which my dislike is founded. Long before it had taken place, my opinion of you was decided. Your character was unfolded in the recital which I received many months ago from Mr. Wickham. On this subject, what can you have to say? In what imaginary act of friendship can you here defend yourself? or under what misrepresentation can you here impose upon others?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: You take an eager interest in that gentleman’s concerns.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Who that knows what his misfortunes have been can help feeling an interest in him?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: His misfortunes! repeated Darcy, contemptuously--yes, his misfortunes have been great indeed.
